items.stimulus:
The following text is from a play. Ines, a visiting birdwatcher, has just told her uncle Tomas that the swallows nesting in his barn are a nuisance and should be driven off.

TOMAS: A nuisance? Each of those birds eats hundreds of flies a day. Before they came, my cows were tormented from June to September. Drive the swallows off, and the flies will be back before summer ends. I would sooner lose the barn roof than lose those birds.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ines argues that the swallows in the barn are a nuisance and should be removed.
Tomas argues that the swallows are valuable because they keep flies away from his cows.
Tomas worries that the swallows nesting in the barn will soon damage its roof.
Tomas claims that swallows eat more flies than any other bird in the region.
items.explanation: The introduction tells you Tomas is answering Ines's complaint. In plain English, his lines say the swallows eat the flies that used to bother his cows, and the flies will come back if the birds leave. His last line, which says he would rather lose the roof than the birds, sums up that view: the swallows are worth keeping.

A.why: You summarized the other character. The introduction gives Ines's view, but the question is about Tomas's speech, and he argues against her.

C.why: You read 'I would sooner lose the barn roof' literally. Tomas isn't predicting damage. He is saying how much more he values the birds than the roof.

D.why: Tomas says each swallow eats hundreds of flies, but he never compares swallows with other birds. You added a claim the text doesn't make.

The following text is from a play set in an English weaving town in 1830. A merchant has just told Hannah, a hand-loom weaver, that the new power looms will soon put her out of work.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

Hannah is unsure whether machine-made cloth keeps its pattern after many washings.

The following text is adapted from a novel. A student has just called the speech of a coastal fishing village "bad English." Her professor responds.

"Bad? Listen to how the fishermen say 'I be mending' for work they do every day and 'I'm mending' for a single job. That is not carelessness, my dear. It marks a difference standard English cannot show in so few words. Their grammar is not broken; it is simply different from ours."

The professor notes that the fishermen mostly discuss mending their nets and boats.

C.why: The professor says standard English can't make this one distinction as briefly. He never claims it is less expressive than every dialect.

The following text is from a play. Two researchers are diving above a reef. Leo, a new assistant, has just surfaced to report that the coral below has turned white and must be dead.

DR. OKAFOR: White, yes, but not dead. Coral turns pale when warm water forces out the algae living inside it. If the water cools within a few weeks, those algae can return. Dead coral is soon covered with seaweed. Tell me, did you see any seaweed down there?

C.why: You missed the hedges. Dr. Okafor says the algae 'can' return 'if' the water cools within weeks. That is a possibility, not a promise.

The following text is from a play set in a nineteenth-century village. Hannah, a well-digger, answers a neighbor who asks why she will not dig a new well beside the tannery.

NEIGHBOR: The ground is soft there. Thou mayst dig it in half the time.
HANNAH: Soft ground drinks whatever is poured upon it. If the tannery's waste sinks into that soil, then the water we draw beneath it will carry the waste back to us. I'll dig farther off and gladly take the longer labor.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

The following text is from a play. Rosa Ferrand, an engineer, speaks to a town councilman who wants a new bridge opened before winter.

COUNCILMAN: The steel is here. The crew is here. Why should we wait?
ROSA: Because the concrete in the piers has not yet cured. Put traffic on it now and it will hold—for a year, perhaps two. Wait a month, and it will hold for my grandchildren's grandchildren.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

Rosa warns that the bridge will fall the moment any traffic is allowed onto it.
Rosa argues that a short delay now will let the bridge last for generations.

B.why: This exaggerates Rosa's warning until it contradicts her. She says the bridge would hold for a year or two, so she does not say it would fail at once.

D.why: You turned one bridge into a general rule. Rosa's objection is about this concrete not having cured, not about winter construction in general.

CAPTAIN: Other charts fill that coast with towns and rivers. Why dost thou leave it bare?

Elias claims that every other chart of that coast was drawn from false reports.

The following text is from a play set at a rural experiment station. Halloway, a farmer, has asked the station chemist, Pryce, why his wheat yields keep falling.
HALLOWAY: I have manured that field every autumn, as my father did. Surely the fault lies in the seed.
PRYCE: Thou mayst change thy seed a dozen times, and still the yield will fall. That field has borne wheat for three generations, and every harvest carried off what the manure never put back. Sow it with clover two seasons, then come ask me about seed.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Halloway insists that his poor harvests must come from faulty seed, since he has manured the field faithfully.
Pryce contends that changing the seed will raise the yield only if it is done many times over several seasons.
Pryce contends that the falling yields come from years of wheat draining the soil rather than from the seed.
Pryce contends that manure has done the field no good and that wheat should be abandoned there permanently.
items.explanation: The introduction tells you Pryce is answering Halloway's question, so Pryce's reply carries the point. In plain English: changing the seed won't help, because three generations of wheat have taken out more than the manure put back, so plant clover for a while. B.why: You read 'a dozen times' literally. Pryce means that no amount of seed-changing will help ('still the yield will fall'). He isn't telling Halloway to do it more often.

The following text is from a play. Two excavators, Corbett and Ines, are examining a buried hearth at a site that published accounts describe as a brief seasonal camp.
CORBETT: A single hearth. Hunters stopped here one autumn, cooked, and moved on. The textbooks say as much.
INES: Then tell me why the clay floor beneath it has been replastered seven times. Travelers passing through don't mend a floor they will never see again. Whoever cooked here came back, year upon year, or never left at all.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

Ines argues that the repeated replastering shows the site was used over a long period rather than once.
items.explanation: The introduction sets up the accepted view, and Ines's reply overturns it. The seven layers of plaster point to people who returned or stayed, because short-term visitors don't repair a floor. Choice D captures that challenge.

A.why: This is Corbett's position, the textbook view Ines argues against. Choosing it means you matched the wrong speaker.

B.why: You took 'tell me why' literally. Ines isn't stuck. She is making a point and already gives the answer: the people came back or never left.

C.why: Ines talks only about the replastered floor and repeated use. Nothing in the text mentions stone houses, so this claims more than the evidence supports.

OSTRANDER: Fronds, aye. But where are the spore cases? Every fern I ever pressed bore them on the leaf's underside, and this leaf is bare as a plate. items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

Ostrander agrees that the fossil's leafy fronds clearly show it to be an ordinary fern.
Ostrander proves that the fossil is the oldest seed-bearing plant collectors have found.
Ostrander argues that the fossil's spore cases reveal it to be a rare variety of fern.
items.explanation: Ostrander admits the leaf has fronds, then points out it has no spore cases, which ferns carry. He asks whether a swelling at the stem's end is a seed, and his 'If it is, then…' sentence holds his claim: it may be a seed plant that only looks like a fern. The word 'if' keeps that claim tentative, and so does choice A.

C.why: Ostrander only says 'if it is' a seed. He proves nothing, and he never claims the plant is the oldest of anything.

The following text is from a translation of a 1911 play. Bram, a fisherman, is speaking with Ilse, a naturalist who has spent several seasons studying the eels of his harbor.

Ilse argues that shrinking catches show the eels are limited, as her records reveal.
Ilse notes that fishermen of Bram's generation use lighter nets than their fathers did.
Ilse warns that the harbor's eels will vanish entirely within the next few years.

In this scene from a play set in 1721, the physician Thomas Ware urges Ann Lisle to let him inoculate her son against smallpox.

LISLE: You would put into him the very sickness I pray he never meets.

WARE: A little of it, madam, given in a quiet house, that he may be spared the whole of it in a crowded street. Mark me, I promise no miracle; a few so treated do fall gravely ill. But of a hundred children who wait, how many more shall I bury?
items.stem: Based on the text, which of the following is NOT a point Ware makes?

Some children who are inoculated go on to become seriously ill.
Inoculation is certain to leave every treated child unharmed.
More children are likely to die if they are left uninoculated.

In this scene from a play, the city planner Rosa Imari responds to Councilman Lyle Brandt, who supports building a highway through the Eastgate district.

BRANDT: The road will carry forty thousand cars a day. That is progress you can count.

IMARI: Count them, then. But count too the shops whose doors will face a wall, and the children who must cross six lanes to reach school. I do not say the city needs no road. I say that if we measure progress only in cars, we will build a city easy to drive through and hard to live in.
items.stem: Based on the text, which of the following is NOT a point Imari makes?
choices: The road would harm the shops that sit along its route.
The road would make some children's walk to school riskier.
Judging the road only by its traffic would mislead the city.
The city should abandon its plan to build any new road.
items.explanation: Imari states directly, "I do not say the city needs no road." Her objection is to measuring progress only by traffic. She is not objecting to roads in general. Choice D credits her with a position she explicitly rejects, so it is the one point she does not make.

A.why: You read "shops whose doors will face a wall" as background description rather than as part of her argument. In plain English she is saying the road would cut those shops off. That is a cost she wants counted, so this is a point she makes.

B.why: You may have tied the six lanes to Brandt's traffic figures and treated this as his detail. Imari is the one who raises the children crossing six lanes to reach school. She uses it as a danger the road would create, so this is a point she makes.

C.why: You skipped the conditional that carries her claim: "if we measure progress only in cars, we will build a city... hard to live in." This is the subtype's trap: older-sounding "if... then" phrasing hiding a simple point. This choice states that point.
